stimulus.source_note: Verbatim excerpts from Henry Cabot Lodge, Senate speech on the League of Nations, August 12, 1919 (public domain). Article X paraphrased from the Covenant of the League of Nations.
stimulus.text:
Senator Henry Cabot Lodge, speech in the Senate on the League of Nations, August 12, 1919 (verbatim excerpts):

"You may call me selfish if you will, conservative or reactionary, or use any other harsh adjective you see fit to apply, but an American I was born and an American I have remained all my life. I can never be anything else but an American, and I must think of the United States first, and when I think of the United States first in an arrangement like this, I am thinking of what is best for the world."

. . .

"I have never had but one allegiance — I cannot divide it now."

The League Covenant's Article X asked member nations to respect and preserve each other's territory against outside attack. Lodge proposed reservations stating that only Congress could commit American forces to such action.

rationales.A: Both groups opposed the treaty as Wilson presented it. The difference is about what each group would accept, not about supporting Wilson's points.
rationales.B: Background from the books: the reservationists, led by Lodge, would vote for the treaty if the Senate attached conditions protecting Congress's war power and the Monroe Doctrine. The irreconcilables refused the treaty and the League in any form.
rationales.C: The irreconcilables wanted no League membership at all, and no senator in the debate was arguing for Germany to join the League.
rationales.D: The reservationists did not oppose membership outright; they wanted conditions. The Monroe Doctrine was something Lodge wanted to protect, not oppose.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what each group would accept. The reservationists would accept the treaty with conditions attached.
2. Ask what the other group would accept. The irreconcilables would accept nothing: no treaty, no League.
3. Name the difference in one line. One group bargained over conditions; the other refused the whole arrangement.
Remember: when two groups oppose the same measure, sort them by what each would accept, not by what each opposes.
